beats.intro: Chapter eight, lesson two. The laws of thermodynamics. [[fire]]A campfire gives off light and heat, and then the wood is gone. Where did its energy go? [[cells]]Every cell faces the same question, as it runs its chemical pathways. [[strip]]Here is our pathway strip again. [[drop]]This time we follow the energy as it moves along it, and the two rules that decide where that energy can go.
beats.systems: [[def]]Thermodynamics is the study of energy transformations. To study one, we pick a piece of the universe and call it the system. Everything else is its surroundings. [[iso]]In an isolated system, nothing crosses the boundary, neither energy nor matter. Think of a sealed, perfectly insulated flask. [[open]]In an open system, energy and matter can both be transferred between the system and its surroundings. [[org]]Organisms are open systems. A cell takes in food and gives off heat and waste all day long.
beats.first: [[law1]]The first law of thermodynamics says that the energy of the universe is constant. Energy can be transferred and transformed, but it cannot be created or destroyed. [[fruit]]Take a piece of fruit. It holds chemical energy in its bonds. [[change]]When a cell breaks it down, that chemical energy is transformed into other forms, such as movement and heat. [[total]]Add everything up afterward, and the total is exactly what we began with. The energy changed form, but it did not disappear.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which statement matches the first law?
beats.second: [[law2]]If the total never changes, why can't a cell reuse the same energy forever? The second law answers. During every energy transfer or transformation, some energy becomes unusable, and is often lost as heat. [[heat]]A cell burns fruit sugar. Part of the energy does work. Part leaves as heat, and the cell cannot use that heat to do more work. [[entropy]]Heat is the random motion of molecules, so it adds disorder. Entropy is a measure of disorder, and the second law says that every energy transfer or transformation increases the entropy of the universe. [[dots]]Dots in neat rows scatter easily. They never march back into rows by themselves.
beats.spont: [[spont]]A spontaneous process occurs without energy input. Water runs downhill. A sugar cube dissolves in tea. An iron nail rusts. [[speed]]Spontaneous does not mean fast. Rusting takes years, and an explosion takes a moment. Both are spontaneous. [[rule]]For a process to occur without energy input, it must increase the entropy of the universe. [[reverse]]The reverse, scattered dots lining up in rows, would lower the entropy, so it will not happen unless something pays for it.
beats.q2: Quick check. What is true of every spontaneous process?
beats.order: [[cell]]But wait. A cell builds ordered things, proteins, membranes, a whole organism, from loose, less ordered materials. Does that break the second law? [[no]]No. The cell is not the whole universe. [[pay]]To build order, it spends energy, and it releases heat and waste, which scatter outward. The disorder around the cell grows by more than the order inside it. So the entropy of the universe still rises. [[flow]]On the scale of an ecosystem, energy flows in as light, and exits as heat.
beats.example: [[start]]Let's follow one worked example. A cell breaks down a glucose molecule, and uses its chemical energy. [[split]]The first law says all of that energy is accounted for. The work done, plus the heat released, equals what the glucose gave up. [[heat2]]The second law says the heat share can never be zero. So a cell can never turn all of the glucose's energy into work. [[co2]]And the glucose breaks into smaller, more scattered pieces, carbon dioxide and water, which adds disorder too.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]First law. Energy is conserved. It changes form, and never vanishes. [[w2]]Second law. Every transformation loses some energy as heat, and entropy rises. [[w3]]Spontaneous processes need no energy input, and they raise the entropy of the universe. [[w4]]Cells are open systems. They build order, and pay for it with heat and disorder. Now try the practice.
